newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn proposes petrol, tobacco tax increases-paper.
newsitem.headline: Bonn proposes petrol, tobacco tax increases-paper.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) have proposed raising taxes on petrol, tobacco and alcohol to fill Bonn's gaping budget holes and to help it qualify for the European Union's planned single currency, a newspaper said.

The Handlesblatt business daily, without naming its sources, said on Tuesday night ahead of publication on Wednesday that the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), made the proposal at a crisis meeting of the coalition on Tuesday to find ways to balance the budget.

Junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) have vehemently opposed any increases in taxation, but the coalition needs to find new ways to plug its budget defict after it was forced to back down on a plan to revalue Bundesbank assets.

The CDU/CSU union said an increase in petrol taxes could bring in an extra 800 million marks ($463 million) and raising taxes on each cigarette by one pfennig would raise 1.35 billion marks, Handlesblatt said.
The union also said it could raise 170 million marks from higher taxes on alcohol and 250 million by limiting the way companies registered losses on their balance sheets.

Earlier, coalition deputies at the meeting said Finance Minister Theo Waigel told them he was 19 billion marks short in his 1997 budget and Kohl backed him up in plans for spending cuts and more privatisations.
Waigel told deputies in the closed-door meeting he expected to take in 10 billion marks from sales of Bonn's shares in Deutsche Telekom and another three billion from cuts in planned spending.
The minister said Bonn could also increase revenues by selling some of its holdings in Lufthansa, the Postbank, highway petrol concessions and other properties.

The deputies said Kohl said he shared responsibility for the current situation and threw his support solidly behind Waigel, saying he would rebuff all criticism of him during a parliamentary debate on the budget on Thursday. He urged them to close ranks behind Waigel. ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
